heading_overrides.A Deaf Man Is Opened: A Deaf Man Hears and Speaks Clearly
heading_overrides.Peter Confesses Jesus as the Christ: Peter Confesses Jesus as the Messiah

notes: The quotation echoes Isaiah 6:9–10. The Greek connects the parables with not perceiving and not turning back. ‘So that’ and ‘lest’ retain the difficult wording; the relation of purpose and result remains a matter for interpretation.
The Greek says ‘smallest of all the seeds on earth.’ This translation retains the saying’s superlative rather than adding ‘among’ or limiting it to seeds a particular farmer used.
vocabulary: Mystery or secret; here something given to the hearers.
Word or message; repeated throughout the explanation of the sower.
A container used for measuring grain, here placed over a lamp.
On its own, without the sower directing the growth.

notes: The reply shifts from ‘my’ to ‘we,’ and the next sentence has one speaker pleading for ‘them.’ These shifts are retained.
‘Possessed by demons’ translates the narrator’s description. It is not a modern medical diagnosis.
The same Greek verb can mean ‘save’ or ‘heal.’ The immediate setting concerns bodily healing; the wider sense of rescue is not excluded.
The verb rendered ‘overheard’ can also mean ‘disregarded.’ Either reading has Jesus responding to the report of the girl’s death.
‘Talitha koum’ is an Aramaic expression retained in the Greek narrative, which then gives its meaning.
vocabulary: Legion, a large Roman military unit; the name here is explained by ‘we are many.’
Decapolis, literally ‘Ten Cities,’ the name of a region.
Save, rescue, or heal; here ‘has made you well.’
Believe or trust; related to ‘faith’ in verse 34.

notes: ‘In the prescribed way’ renders an uncertain expression, literally ‘with the fist.’ It may describe how the hands were washed; ‘carefully’ is another interpretation. The exact gesture is uncertain.

These verses are the narrator’s explanation of the customs at issue. The broad phrase ‘all the Jews’ is retained as part of that description, not expanded into a claim about every Jewish community in every period.
Verse 16 is absent from the Greek text followed here. The numbering gap is retained.

The closing words are literally ‘cleansing all foods.’ The masculine participle is taken here as a comment about Jesus and his teaching. Another interpretation connects it with the process of digestion and elimination.
‘Envy’ renders the expression ‘evil eye,’ which can suggest a begrudging or ungenerous attitude.
‘Gentile’ is literally ‘Greek’ here, in contrast to Jewish identity. ‘Syrophoenician by birth’ gives the woman’s more specific background.

The word for ‘dogs’ is a diminutive that can refer to small or household dogs. This does not remove the contrast between children and dogs in the exchange. ‘Lord’ can also be a respectful address, ‘Sir.’
vocabulary: Common or defiled; here contrasted with hands washed according to the tradition.
Corban, a gift dedicated to God; the designation here affects what can be given to a parent.
An Aramaic command, explained in the narrative as ‘Be opened.’

notes: Mark uses two words for baskets. The larger baskets in this feeding and verse 20 translate spyris; the baskets in verse 19 and the earlier feeding translate kophinos.
The Greek uses a shortened oath formula, literally ‘if a sign will be given.’ Here it expresses a firm refusal, not uncertainty about whether a sign will come.
The man’s sight returns in two stages. His first report and Jesus’ second touch are both retained.
‘Must’ preserves the stated necessity without explaining its basis. ‘After three days’ follows Mark’s wording here.
The same Greek word, psychē, is rendered ‘life’ throughout these sayings. It can also refer to the self or soul; the translation does not impose a separation of body and soul on the passage.
vocabulary: Yeast or leaven; retained as the warning’s image without supplying its interpretation.
Son of Man, Jesus’ recurring self-designation.
Life, self, or soul; here repeated in the save–lose and gain–forfeit sayings.

notes: The Greek says that he ‘could not,’ not merely that he chose not to. It then names the healings that did occur.
Mark explicitly permits a staff and sandals. These instructions are not adjusted to match the other Gospel accounts.
‘A testimony to them’ can carry the force of testimony against them in this setting.
The Greek wording followed here identifies the girl as Herodias’s own daughter; it does not give the girl a personal name.
The fourth watch was the last part of the night, roughly three to six in the morning. ‘He intended to pass by them’ is retained without explaining his intention.
‘It is I’ translates egō eimi, literally ‘I am.’ It can serve as ordinary self-identification; possible scriptural echoes are left open.
The final pronoun may refer to Jesus or to his garment or its fringe. The preceding request specifically concerns touching the fringe.
vocabulary: Tunic, a basic garment worn beneath an outer cloak.
Apostle or one sent out; here the returning Twelve.
Denarius, a Roman coin; two hundred are named here.
Harden or make unresponsive; the Greek describes their heart as hardened.
